title: Overcoming Animosity Toward a Team Member
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece examines the psychology of leader animosity toward team members — the deep-seated dislike or resentment that accumulates over time and colors every subsequent interaction — and offers a practical path toward resolution. The article distinguishes between two roots of animosity: a specific event (betrayal, humiliation, rejection) and accumulated friction arising from psychological, ideological, or value differences perceived as threatening. Most animosity, the article argues, comes from the second source, which means it is fundamentally a problem of interpretation: the leader has developed a pattern of reading the team member's actions as intentionally harmful rather than seeing them in a more generous frame. Psychologists' concept of 'negative sentiment override' — where even neutral behavior gets filtered through accumulated negative impressions — explains why animosity is self-reinforcing once established. The article argues that resolving animosity starts with the leader, not the team member, and that the path is reinterpretation: learning to separate the team member's behavior from the leader's attribution of malicious intent.
points: Most leader animosity does not come from a single betrayal but from accumulated day-to-day friction interpreted through an increasingly negative lens — and interpretation, not behavior, is where the leader can intervene.

Negative sentiment override is the psychological mechanism that makes animosity self-reinforcing: once established, even neutral or positive behavior by the team member gets read as further evidence of their flaws.

The starting point for resolution is accepting that the team member does not need to change — the leader's task is to change their own interpretive frame, which is something the leader has complete agency over.

Animosity rooted in value or personality differences is particularly common because difference itself is often experienced unconsciously as a threat, triggering a defensive interpretation pattern that has nothing to do with actual workplace harm.

The practical discipline is learning to stop interpreting the team member's actions as intentionally harmful and personally directed — a discipline that requires active effort because the negative interpretation pattern is automatic and reinforced by attention bias.
quotes: Without necessarily meaning to, leaders sometimes hold a grudge. They can let their negative impressions and feelings toward a team member influence how they engage with them.
The good news is that fixing it doesn’t require the team member to change at all. Animosity is a deep-seated dislike or resentment toward another person.
Learning how to overcome this feeling is essential to effective leadership. The first is a discrete event where the leader feels deeply wronged, betrayed, deceived, humiliated, or rejected.

Much more commonly, leaders feel animosity because of psychological, ideological, and value differences between themselves and their team members — differences perceived as a threat, no matter how exaggerated, irrational, or mistaken that perception turns out to be. In those cases, the animosity is less about what actually happened than about what the leader believes it to mean.

Each unpleasant exchange makes the next one easier to read as further proof of the other person’s flaws, until the leader is no longer responding to what the team member actually did but to an accumulated impression of who they are. Psychologists call this negative sentiment override, and once it takes hold, even neutral or well-intentioned behavior gets filtered through that lens.

Leaders will likely find some of the actions and behaviors of their team members annoying or irritating at times. But what commonly turns ordinary annoyance into animosity isn’t the behavior or its repetition, but the interpretation the leader assigns to it.

This means it can be addressed by changing how the leader interprets the behavior, independent of whether the team member changes anything at all. Leaders who want to overcome their animosity must learn to stop interpreting a team member’s actions as intentionally harmful and personally aimed at them.
